text: You get an array nums of distinct integers. Return all possible permutations. Any order is fine.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — here order matters. One, two and two, one are two different answers. And each element is used exactly once in one permutation. Is that right?
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and six, each value is between negative ten and ten, and all values are distinct.

OK. Since the values are distinct, I don't need to handle duplicates. And n at most six means at most seven hundred twenty answers, so listing them all is fine. Let me run through the example. One, two, three gives six permutations — that's three factorial. Zero, one gives two, and a single one gives just itself.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of the backtracking template: fill a path one slot at a time, recurse, then undo. But there's one key difference. When order doesn't matter, like choosing a group, the loop starts at a start index s, so every path is increasing and two, one never shows up. Here order does matter, so every slot must be able to take any element. So the loop always starts from zero, and I need another way to stop reuse: a used array.

Here's the plan. One: if the path has n elements, record it and return. Two: otherwise loop i from zero, and skip any index that's already used. Three: mark it used, push it, recurse, then pop it and clear the mark. The loop decides which element goes in this slot, and used makes sure each one goes in only once. One thing worth flagging — I changed two pieces of state, so the undo has two parts: pop back and used of i equals false. If I forget either one, the next branch sees a dirty state. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Permute just sets up the answer list, an empty path and a used array, then calls dfs. In dfs, a full path gets copied into the answer; otherwise the loop runs from zero, skips used indices, and does the set, push, recurse, pop, clear sequence. Path and used are passed by reference, so there's one shared copy of each, and every change is undone right after the recursive call returns. I only copy path when I record an answer. The undo order mirrors the do order: set used, push; then pop, clear used.

Let's dry-run the code with one, two, three — expected all six permutations. The row that matters is call seven: after the whole branch starting with one returns, used is back to all false, so two can go first and one is free again for the second slot. That only works because both undos ran. It takes sixteen calls, one plus three plus six plus six, and gives all six. That matches. Corner cases: zero, one gives both orders in five calls. Drop the used check, and one, two gives four lists with reuse. Forget either undo, and one, two returns only one, two. A start-index loop also returns only one, two.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of n times n factorial. There are n factorial answers, and copying each one costs n. The call count is one plus n plus n times n minus one, up to n factorial, which is still bounded by a constant times n factorial. The space complexity is O of n extra for the recursion stack, path, and used, not counting the output. In the worst-case scenario, n is six: seven hundred twenty answers and one thousand nine hundred fifty-seven calls, in about fifty microseconds.
Can you do it without the used array?

Yes — the swap version. I keep nums from zero to k as the fixed prefix, and nums from k to n as the unused pool. For slot k, I swap each nums of i with i at least k into position k, recurse on k plus one, then swap back. The array itself is the used set, so there's no extra array and no path, and the undo is one part. It makes the same number of calls: sixteen for n equals three, and one thousand nine hundred fifty-seven for n equals six. It's a bit faster at n equals six, thirty-two versus fifty microseconds, same Big-O. The trade-off: the output order is not the same as the used version, but any order is allowed here.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why the loop starts at zero — order matters — and contrasted it with the start index used when order doesn't matter. You treated the undo as two parts, and had a one, two counterexample for each missing piece. And you knew the swap version keeps the same call count while dropping the extra array. Good work.
